# PostgreSQL Auto-generated Key Backfill

PostgreSQL supports JDBC generated keys and also native `INSERT ... RETURNING <column>`. For single-row INSERTs, both methods usually work; for multi-row INSERTs requiring per-row primary key backfill, `RETURNING` better expresses PostgreSQL's native capabilities.

```sql
INSERT INTO user_info (name, age, email)
VALUES (?, ?, ?)
RETURNING id
```

Multi-row INSERTs can also return multiple primary keys at once:

```sql
INSERT INTO user_info (name, age, email)
VALUES (?, ?, ?), (?, ?, ?), (?, ?, ?)
RETURNING id
```

The return value of this SQL manifests as the `ResultSet` returned by the current execution.

## Lambda / BaseMapper

Lambda and BaseMapper INSERT SQL is generated by dbVisitor based on object mapping, so the PostgreSQL dialect can choose `RETURNING` for multi-row primary key backfill scenarios and backfill primary keys from the current `ResultSet`.

```java title='Read backfilled primary key after Lambda insert'
UserInfo user = new UserInfo();
user.setName("mali");
user.setAge(18);

LambdaTemplate lambda = ...
int rows = lambda.insert(UserInfo.class)
                 .applyEntity(user)
                 .executeSumResult();

Integer id = user.getId();
```

```java title='Read backfilled primary key after BaseMapper insert'
BaseMapper<UserInfo> mapper = session.createBaseMapper(UserInfo.class);

UserInfo user = new UserInfo();
user.setName("mali");
user.setAge(18);

int rows = mapper.insert(user);
Integer id = user.getId();
```

For multi-row inserts requiring primary key backfill, the PostgreSQL dialect can generate SQL like:

```sql
INSERT INTO user_info (name, age)
VALUES (?, ?), (?, ?), (?, ?)
RETURNING id
```

## Mapper XML

Mapper XML is hand-written SQL; dbVisitor does not automatically append `RETURNING`. To backfill primary keys via PostgreSQL `RETURNING`, you must explicitly write `RETURNING` in the SQL and declare that generated keys are read from the current result set.

```xml title='PostgreSQL RETURNING'
<insert id="insertUser"
        useGeneratedKeys="true"
        keyProperty="id"
        keyColumn="id"
        generatedKeySource="resultSet">
    INSERT INTO user_info (name, age, email)
    VALUES (#{name}, #{age}, #{email})
    RETURNING id
</insert>
```

Multi-column backfill should also list them explicitly:

```xml
<insert id="insertOrder"
        useGeneratedKeys="true"
        keyProperty="id,orderNo"
        keyColumn="id,order_no"
        generatedKeySource="resultSet">
    INSERT INTO user_order (user_id, amount)
    VALUES (#{userId}, #{amount})
    RETURNING id, order_no
</insert>
```

`generatedKeySource="resultSet"` means generated keys are read from the current `ResultSet`, suitable for use with PostgreSQL `RETURNING`.

## Annotation Mapper

In annotations, the user is likewise responsible for writing PostgreSQL-specific syntax:

```java
@Insert(
    value = """
        INSERT INTO user_info (name, age, email)
        VALUES (#{name}, #{age}, #{email})
        RETURNING id
        """,
    useGeneratedKeys = true,
    keyProperty = "id",
    keyColumn = "id",
    generatedKeySource = GeneratedKeySource.ResultSet
)
int insertUser(UserInfo user);
```

If not using `RETURNING`, continue using regular JDBC generated keys:

```java
@Insert(
    value = "INSERT INTO user_info (name, age) VALUES (#{name}, #{age})",
    useGeneratedKeys = true,
    keyProperty = "id",
    keyColumn = "id"
)
int insertUser(UserInfo user);
```

## ON CONFLICT

PostgreSQL's `ON CONFLICT` is a conflict-handling syntax, not equivalent to a regular INSERT. When hand-writing SQL, if you need to return primary keys after conflict handling, also explicitly write `RETURNING`:

```xml
<insert id="upsertUser"
        useGeneratedKeys="true"
        keyProperty="id"
        keyColumn="id"
        generatedKeySource="resultSet">
    INSERT INTO user_info (id, name, age)
    VALUES (#{id}, #{name}, #{age})
    ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE
    SET name = EXCLUDED.name,
        age = EXCLUDED.age
    RETURNING id
</insert>
```

When Lambda / BaseMapper generates `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`, dbVisitor avoids writing conflict key columns into `SET`.

## Dialect Strategy

PostgreSQL's current strategy is as follows:

| Scenario | GeneratedKeyStrategy |
| --- | --- |
| No backfill columns | `JdbcBatch` |
| `Into` + with backfill columns | `MultiValuesResultSet` |
| `Ignore` + with backfill columns | `OneByOne` |
| `Update` + with backfill columns | `MultiValuesResultSet` |

`DuplicateKeyStrategy.Ignore` uses `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, not requiring a primary key column list; `DuplicateKeyStrategy.Update` uses `ON CONFLICT (<primary key>) DO UPDATE`, requiring primary key columns and at least one non-primary key column that is updatable.

## selectKey

To completely avoid differences between JDBC generated keys and `RETURNING`, you can use `selectKey` / `@SelectKeySql` to first read the sequence value, then execute the INSERT.

```xml
<insert id="insertUser">
    <selectKey keyProperty="id" order="BEFORE">
        SELECT nextval('user_info_id_seq')
    </selectKey>
    INSERT INTO user_info (id, name, age)
    VALUES (#{id}, #{name}, #{age})
</insert>
```

This approach is suitable when the business wants to obtain the primary key before executing the INSERT.

## Design Principles

- Lambda / BaseMapper: SQL is generated by the framework; the PostgreSQL dialect can generate multi-row `VALUES` and `RETURNING`.
- XML / Annotation: SQL is written by the user; dbVisitor does not automatically append `RETURNING`; users must explicitly write `RETURNING`.
- Session / JDBC raw SQL: executed faithfully, not guessing whether the current `ResultSet` represents generated keys.
- General documentation: see [Generated Keys](../../guides/core/mapper/annotation_insert#generated-keys).
